items.title: Topic Eleven Opens: Who Is the True Brahmin?

items.zh: 應作婆羅門，謂斷無縱逸，求棄捨諸欲，不悕望此有。
items.en: One should become a brahmin: cutting off all indulgence, seeking to relinquish every desire, hoping for no further existence here.

items.zh: 若更有所作，非真婆羅門。當知婆羅門，於所作已辦。諸身分劬勞，未極底未度。已得度、住陸，無勤、到彼岸。天！汝今當知，此喻真梵志。謂永盡諸漏，得常委、靜慮。彼永斷一切愁憂及熾燃，恒住於正念，亦常心解脫。
items.en: One who still has more left to do is no true brahmin. Know that the brahmin is one whose task is already accomplished. One still toiling with every limb has not yet reached the bottom, not yet crossed; one who has crossed stands now on dry land, reaching the far shore with no further effort. Deity, know now: this is the true likeness of the genuine seeker of purity — one who has exhausted all corruptions forever, one who has attained constant diligence, or one who has attained meditative absorption. Such a one has forever cut off all sorrow and burning, abides always in right mindfulness, and is forever liberated in mind.

items.zh: 今此頌中，顯示彼天依於世俗諸婆羅門，為世尊說。謂有種姓諸婆羅門，自號我為真實梵志。計梵世間為最究竟，悕求梵世，安住於色，常勤精進，心無懈倦。恒樂遠離，寂靜閑居，減省睡眠，修習靜定，為斷事欲及煩惱欲。由彼種姓諸婆羅門，計梵世間以為究竟，悕望梵世，不求欲有。又顯如來依第一義諸婆羅門，而報彼天。若婆羅門作所作已，數復應作，更有勝上所應作事，當知此非真婆羅門。若婆羅門證婆羅門所應作事，超登一切薩迦耶岸，安住陸地，當知此是真婆羅門。由此顯示學與無學皆婆羅門。學有二種。謂於欲界或未離欲，或已離欲。未離欲者，未得源底，未到彼岸，於二種法猶未具足。一、未得內心勝奢摩他；二、雖已得，增上慧法毘鉢舍那未善清淨。由闕內心奢摩他故，乘如所得聖道浮囊，為證內心奢摩他故，運動如足勇猛精進。又復為令增上慧法毘鉢舍那善清淨故，運動如手勇猛精進。彼於如是勤精進時，離欲界欲，如得源底；證阿羅漢，如到彼岸。已離欲者，證得內心勝奢摩他，亦得善淨毘鉢舍那。唯為進斷上分諸結，發勤精進，非諸身分。若已越度，成阿羅漢，所作已辦，離勤功用，名住陸地，已到彼岸。此則顯示諸婆羅門，依第一義略有三種。二是有學，一是無學。若已究竟到於彼岸諸婆羅門，名永盡漏。若未離欲一切身分勤精進者，名得常委。若已離欲得源底者，名得靜慮。得靜慮者，永斷一切下分結故，已斷貪欲及瞋恚品所有一切愁憂熾燃。永盡漏者，永斷修斷諸煩惱故，已善修習四種念住，恒住正念及心解脫。彼非作已數數更作，亦無增勝所應作事，是故說彼名第一義真婆羅門。

blocks.text: A short day. A deva, speaking for brahmins of the caste, describes the true brahmin; the Buddha answers with the brahmin "in the ultimate sense". The explanation (0377b26–0378a02) is **untranslated**.

The deva: one should become a brahmin, cutting off indulgence, seeking to relinquish desire, hoping for no further existence. The Buddha: "One who still has more left to do is no true brahmin. The brahmin is one whose task is already accomplished. One still toiling with every limb has not yet reached the bottom, not yet crossed."

items: **The deva's brahmin.** Brahmins of the caste call themselves true brahmins. They take the Brahmā world as the final goal, practise diligently, live in solitude, sleep little, and cultivate concentration, but only to reach the Brahmā world.

**The Buddha's brahmin.** A brahmin who has done what is to be done and still has more to do is not a true brahmin. One who has done it all, "crossed beyond all identity to the far shore and stands on dry land", is.
**Three kinds.** In the ultimate sense, trainees and those beyond training are all brahmins, of three kinds:

A trainee **not yet free of desire**, "toiling with every limb", has neither reached the bottom nor crossed. Lacking calm, one "rides the float of the noble path" and strives with the feet for calm; for clear insight, one strives with the hands. Venerable Miào Jìng: the feet are diligence in concentration, the hands diligence in wisdom. Master Cháng Bǎi calls this person "constantly diligent".
A trainee **free of desire** has calm and pure insight, "has reached the bottom", and strives only to cut the higher fetters: "attained meditation".

The **arhat**, who has crossed and stands on dry land: "corruptions ended". Having cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, such a one has nothing further to do, and is "the true brahmin in the ultimate sense".

blocks.text: The Buddha does not reject the word "brahmin"; he redefines it. Its value is not in birth or ritual but in what has been accomplished inwardly. He does the same with "noble" (ārya) and "pure".

quiz.q: The deity says "one should become a brahmin." How does the Buddha respond?
options: a brahmin must be nobly born
one who still has more to do is no true brahmin; the brahmin is one whose task is done
quiz.why: "One who still has more left to do is no true brahmin. Know that the brahmin is one whose task is already accomplished." Master Cháng Bǎi: the third kind of brahmin is the noble one who has attained the fruit of the path.

quiz.q: Among three kinds of brahmin, what is the third, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: an accomplished practitioner — a noble one who has attained the fruit of the path
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the third kind is one accomplished in practice — only a noble one who has realised the fruit of the path is called a brahmin. He adds that freedom from desire is called 梵 and 志 is the mind, so a brahmin is also called 梵志.

quiz.q: The English joins "toiling with every limb, not yet at the bottom, not yet across" and "crossed, standing on dry land" into one person. How does Venerable Miào Jìng read "not at the bottom, not across"?
options: not at the bottom means no concentration yet; not across means wisdom incomplete — a trainee not free of desire, distinct from the arhat on dry land
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: not reaching the bottom means not having attained concentration; not reaching the far shore means wisdom is not complete. The lecture distinguishes the trainee not yet free of desire from the one beyond training "on dry land"; the English "such is the one who has crossed" merges them.

quiz.q: "謂永盡諸漏，得常委靜慮" is rendered "or who abides in constant, thorough diligence in meditation." How does Master Cháng Bǎi divide it?
options: "constant diligence" is the trainee not yet free of desire (first and second fruits); "meditation" is another, already free of desire — the English merges them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the second kind is "attaining constant diligence" — trainees not yet free of desire, stream-enterers and once-returners. The lecture separates those who have exhausted the corruptions, those of constant diligence, and those of meditation into three; the English merges the last two.

quiz.q: What image does Venerable Miào Jìng use for the "toil of every limb," and how does it differ from the note's swimming image?
options: climbing — the hands' grip stands for diligence in insight, the feet's for diligence in concentration
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the climbing motion of the hands stands for diligence in wisdom, in insight; the climbing of the feet stands for diligence in concentration. The note uses a swimmer's limbs; the assignments match, but the image differs.
